book.title: The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up
book.author: Marie Kondo

confidence_note: Core quotes (the criterion 'whether or not it gives you a thrill of pleasure when you touch it', 'keep things because you love them, not just because', the two causes, the three approaches, worldly desires decreasing, tidying as a tool) come from a summary that quotes the English edition. Thanking unused clothes and gifts for the joy they gave is from secondary quote collections (medium). Year is the Japanese original (2011); the English edition is 2014. The old text's client dialogue about a blouse and the 'energy giving or taking' framing are not in the book and were dropped.
facts: Kondo thought about storage from age five, discovered discarding as a teenager, and began treating belongings as if alive in high school; she later tidied clients' homes.
Criterion: pick up each item; 'whether or not it gives you a thrill of pleasure when you touch it'. She also phrases it as 'speak to your heart' or 'moves you'.
'Keep things because you love them, not just because.' Two reasons people can't let go: attachment to the past or fear for the future.
An item bought and never used gave joy when bought and completed its role; a gift's role is to be received; thank the item for the joy and let it go.
Three approaches to possessions: face them now, face them sometime, or avoid them until the day we die.
Discarding comes before deciding where to store; items of one category are gathered in one place first.
After tidying, many clients say their worldly desires decreased. 'Tidying is just a tool, not the final destination.'
scene_details: a sweater held in both hands
a pile of one category on the floor
thanking a never-worn shirt before letting it go
tension: We keep many things that give us nothing, and reasons don't help us decide.
opening_idea: Open on the never-worn item being thanked, or on the hand-held test, without naming the author.

lessons.idea: Judge an object while holding it; the feeling is more honest than the reasons.
lessons.anchor: The touch criterion and the thank-you ritual.

reflect_final: Which object at home do you keep only from attachment to the past or fear for the future?

use_cases.situation: Clearing a wardrobe as a family
use_cases.move: Hold each item; keep what brings joy, thank and bag the rest.
Thank it for the joy on purchase day and let it go.

use_cases.situation: Friend can't part with a disliked gift
use_cases.move: Share Kondo's view that a gift's job ends when received.

pocket_idea: Hold each object; if no joy, thank it for the joy it once gave and let go.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Kondo says a shirt you never wore already did its job the day you bought it.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: The touch test and the thank-you ritual.
